newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli budget passes first parliamentary hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Israeli budget passes first parliamentary hurdle.

text.p: Israel's parliament gave preliminary approval by a slim margin for the government's controversial 1997 budget on Wednesday.
After intense negotiations lasting most of the day aimed at ensuring support from the full coalition, the 120-member parliament approved the budget by a vote of 59-52 on its first reading.
Five coalition members from the Israel ba-Aliya party abstained.

Gesher, a faction in the ruling Likud party led by Foreign Minister David Levy, dropped its opposition to the legislation in return for a letter from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu promising to consider changes in the budget before a final vote in parliament by year's end.

The 190.8 billion shekel budget, which includes 4.8 billion shekels in spending cuts, is being challenged by coalition members who say it hurts lower-income groups. The budget would reduce subsidies for health care and child allowances.
But the government is determined to reduce the budget deficit next year to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product.
The Netanyahu letter spurred protests from opposition parties, who said it constituted an agreement to make changes in the budget and therefore the law required its contents be revealed.
They said they would seek a court order to have the letter published.
Speaking after the vote, Netanyahu played down the importance of any promises made to coalition partners.
"I am committed to preserving the framework of the budget," he said. "I am ready to review several of the social-welfare clauses with the possibility of changing them."

The vigorous debate over the first reading of the budget was unusual, as parliament in past years has saved negotiations and horse-trading for the second and third readings required before any legislation can become law.
Amotz Asa-El, economics editor of The Jerusalem Post, noted that the vote occurred on schedule and said it was not important that less than half of parliament supported the budget.
Asa-El termed most of the opposition to the budget inside the coalition as posturing.
"None of the coalition partners or lobbyists have a real case," he said. "They're all token struggles."
He said the government would hold to current spending ceilings.
"There will be changes inside the budget but not fundamental ones," Asa-El said.
